rv.q: It is, unsurprisingly given its origins, compact and it has bears some of the structural hallmarks of a tyro piece: it’s a little messy, a little rushed and not quite convincingly resolved.
Superb acting, design and direction, plus really fine writing make for a drama that is much more than the sum of its parts.
Strikingly relevant in light of these recent events, Animals Say offers an entertaining and palatable primer of the forces at play in Northern Ireland.
This is an immensely watchable two-hander, buoyed by Ireland's ear for pacey dialogue, which more than papers over the cracks in its plot.
This 70-minute, two man show is a perfect snapshot of human nature, and its flaws and contradictions.
This hugely enjoyable dark comedy is over in a blink.
Superbly acted and staged this production... is one of those rare evenings in the theatre where everything is as it should be.
The team delivers a torrent of laughs whilst demanding that the audience consider shocking truths that underlie Belfast's historic conflicts.
The 70-minute dark comedy is as funny as it is thought-provoking.
What the Animals Say is an entertaining watch with some brilliant performances.
Animals Say is an entertaining, foul-mouthed and frequently hilarious two-hander, elevated by two committed performances.
Still, there are plenty of laughs across a tight 70 minutes and, as a chance to see the foundations of Ireland's later success, it's a worthwhile night out.

cn.t: Ireland's debut play packs visceral punch in its 70-minute runtime, with critics praising its sharp humor and exploration of sectarianism and masculinity, though some note its rough edges and rushed structure as signs of early work.
